hero.name: Kabir
hero.who: a 26-year-old bank clerk in Bhopal who scrolls and snacks late every night

story.b: Kabir finishes his shift at the bank branch near New Market at six, eats dinner with his parents, and then the evening disappears. He lies on his bed with reels playing and a packet of namkeen open beside him. Around eleven he opens a shopping app and adds a pair of earphones he does not need. At one in the morning he finally puts the phone down and feels strangely empty, as if the whole evening happened to someone else. He is not even enjoying it anymore. Each reel is a little less funny than the one before. The next day he is tired at the counter, snaps at a customer over a passbook, and promises himself tonight will be different. It never is.

ask.q: Kabir keeps scrolling and snacking even though he no longer enjoys it. What is the most useful first step for him?
o: Download a calmer app and keep scrolling, just slower content
Start noticing how he actually feels after each quick pleasure, not just before
Blame his weak willpower and promise to try harder tomorrow
ask.why: Swapping apps keeps the same loop running, and blaming willpower only adds shame, which often sends him straight back to the phone. Noticing how he feels afterwards shows him the real cost of the habit. That honest look is where change usually begins.

chapters.take: If a pleasure stops feeling good, start by noticing what it leaves behind.

story.b: On Saturday Kabir watches eight episodes of a thriller in one sitting and finishes a full box of jalebis from the sweet shop downstairs. It feels great for a few hours. On Sunday he wakes up heavy and grey. Nothing seems interesting, not cricket with his cousins, not even his mother's poha. He tries a small experiment and writes in his phone notes how he feels ten minutes after each treat. By evening the pattern is clear. Every big high is followed by a dip that lasts longer than the fun. His cousin Faiz calls and suggests a new series to cheer him up. Kabir looks at his notes and hesitates.

ask.q: Kabir feels flat after a big weekend binge. Faiz suggests another series to lift his mood. What should Kabir do?
o: Watch it, since a new show is the quickest way to feel better
Eat something sweet first, then decide about the show
Skip the next big hit and let the low settle with something ordinary, like a walk
ask.why: The flat feeling is the brain leaning back after a big high. Another binge or a sweet gives a short lift, then an even deeper dip, so the craving grows. Letting the low pass with something simple gives his balance a chance to level out.

chapters.take: Every big high asks for a payback. Chasing more only deepens the low.

story.b: On Monday Kabir decides to count. Every time he reaches for a quick pleasure before lunch, he makes a small tick on the back of a deposit slip. Checking reels in the washroom, a tick. A samosa from the canteen he was not hungry for, a tick. Opening a food app just to look, a tick. A flash sale alert, a tick. By one o'clock there are nineteen. He is shocked, then oddly relieved. He is not a broken person. His phone, his street and his office canteen are all set up to hand him small rewards every few minutes. His colleague Priya says the answer is simply more discipline. Kabir is not so sure.

ask.q: Kabir counted nineteen quick pleasures before lunch. Priya says he just needs more discipline. What is the more helpful way for him to see it?
o: He is surrounded by easy rewards, so he should change his surroundings, not just blame himself
Priya is right, so he should push through on willpower alone
Nineteen is normal these days, so there is nothing to worry about
ask.why: Easy rewards are everywhere now, built to pull him back again and again. Seeing that removes the shame and points to practical fixes. Willpower alone gets worn down by so many small temptations, and calling it normal lets the habit keep running his day.

chapters.take: You are not weak. You are surrounded by rewards made to hook you.

story.b: Kabir picks one habit to pause, the reels, and marks thirty days on the calendar near the fridge. He tells his younger sister Zoya so that someone knows. The first three days are rough. His thumb keeps reaching for an app that is no longer there. He is irritable at work and bored on the bus. On the fourth night he almost reinstalls it, telling himself one quick look cannot hurt. By the second week something shifts. Evening chai on the terrace with his father feels pleasant again. He reads a few pages of an old detective novel. By the end of the month the urge is quieter, and he starts thinking about how he wants to use the app from now on.

ask.q: On day four Kabir is irritable and wants to reinstall the app for one quick look. What should he do?
o: Reinstall it, since feeling this bad means the break is not working
Expect the first days to feel worst, stay with the break, and talk to a doctor if it feels unmanageable
Switch the break to a different, easier habit instead
ask.why: The first days of a break often feel worse before they feel better, so irritation is not a sign of failure. One quick look usually restarts the whole cycle, and switching habits just avoids the hard part. If cravings ever feel truly out of control, a doctor can help.

chapters.take: A break feels worst at the start. Stay long enough for ordinary joys to return.

story.h: The charger in the living room
story.b: After the break, Kabir does not want to rely on willpower again. He decides to put distance between himself and his old traps. His phone now charges in the living room from half past ten, next to his father's radio. He deletes the shopping app, so buying anything takes five slow steps in a browser. Sweets are for Sunday only, bought fresh from the shop and never stored at home. He writes these rules on a sticky note inside his wardrobe door. Some nights he wants the phone badly, but walking out to the living room in front of his parents is enough of a speed bump. Most nights, he simply sleeps.

ask.q: Kabir's cousin Faiz also scrolls till two every night. Which advice from Kabir would help most?
o: Keep the phone close but promise yourself to stop at eleven
Charge the phone outside the bedroom and set a clear cut-off time
Turn the screen grey and keep scrolling in bed as usual
ask.why: A promise made at ten is weakest at midnight, when the phone is already in his hand. A grey screen may help a little, but he is still in bed with the trap. Real distance and a clear rule mean he argues with himself far less.

chapters.take: Do not fight temptation every night. Put a wall between you and it.

story.b: Kabir notices that the best feelings of his month came after effort, not ease. So he adds something hard. Three mornings a week, he walks briskly along the Upper Lake before work, even when the bed feels warm. The first ten minutes are unpleasant. By the end he feels clear and steady for hours, a quieter good feeling than any reel ever gave him. He also tries being fully honest in small things. When his mother asks who finished the laddoos, he admits it was him, at midnight. She laughs. Saying it aloud makes the old habit feel smaller, less like a secret he has to guard.

ask.q: Kabir wants a lasting good feeling, not another quick high. What should he add to his week?
o: A small dose of healthy effort, like a brisk walk, plus honesty about his habits
A shopping treat each Sunday as a reward for staying off reels
A strict plan of hard workouts every single day starting tomorrow
ask.why: Gentle, healthy effort usually feels hard first and good afterwards, and the good part lasts. Honesty stops him hiding habits from himself. A shopping reward swaps one quick hit for another, and a sudden extreme plan tends to collapse. Anyone with health concerns should check with a doctor first.

chapters.take: Effort first, good feeling after. That kind of joy lasts longer.

story.b: Two months later, Kabir still uses his phone, but it no longer uses him. He watches one episode on Friday nights with Zoya and stops there. The shopping app has not come back. Sweets still taste wonderful on Sundays, maybe better than before. At the bank he is less tired, and the customer he once snapped at now asks for his counter by name. In his desk drawer, the deposit slip with nineteen ticks is still there. He keeps it as a reminder. When a new temptation appears, like a game his colleagues are all playing, he asks himself how he will feel ten minutes after, and decides from there.

chapters.take: Balance comes back when you stop chasing every easy high.
